root.note: A variant of deport, from the verbs deporter, desporter, ‘to amuse oneself’.

history: Sport is an Old French word that went to England to have fun and came back to train. Old French deport, with a variant desport, meant pleasure or entertainment, from verbs meaning ‘to amuse oneself’. English took it as disport and then dropped the first syllable: sport, ‘amusement, a game’, from the 15th century. In 1523 the word is used for outdoor exercise, and from 1594 the plural, sports, for athletic contests. French borrowed the English word in 1828, in a journal about horse breeding. Today faire du sport, ‘to do sport’, is everyday French, and a sporty person is sportif, sportive. Note the partitive: je fais du sport, but je fais de la natation.
historyEinfach: Sport comes from an old French word, desport. It meant ‘fun, a game’. English took it and made it shorter: sport. Then French took the English word back, in 1828. Today you say: je fais du sport.

elsewhere.text: English still has disport, ‘to amuse oneself’, beside sport: the long and the short form of the same French word.
